title: Hands-on Lab: Deploy Redwood Private into Customer VPC on Kubernetes
content:
Purpose and audience:
This hands-on lab is built for solutions engineers and customer platform teams running a 3-hour workshop. The goal is to provision Redwood Private in a customer VPC using Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS examples), validate inference end-to-end, and produce a simple rollout/runbook for customer handoff.

Scope and learning objectives:
- Deploy Redwood Private control plane components as Helm charts into a customer-managed k8s cluster inside a VPC subnet.
- Attach an external model-serving node pool (GPU-backed) and demonstrate model routing and fallback to a CPU quantized variant.
- Configure KMS integration for secrets, basic audit logging, and private connectivity (internal LB or NLB with private IP).
- Validate with a sample app: chat UI + backend inference client and an automated load/latency check.

Estimated time: 3.0 hours (setup pre-work recommended: 45–60 minutes)

Prerequisites (customer and workshop):
- Customer provides: cloud account with VPC, at least one k8s cluster (recommended: EKS 1.25+, GKE autopilot or AKS), IAM admin, and subnet CIDR for internal load balancer.
- Workshop host needs: Helm v3, kubectl, eksctl/gcloud/az CLI, a small GPU node pool request (e.g., 1–2 p3/aa2 or A100-equivalent nodes), and access to customer's KMS key.
- Local: aws/gcloud/az credentials configured, Docker for local image build (optional), Python 3.10+ for client tests.

High-level architecture (textual):
1) Customer VPC with private subnets and NAT for outbound (optional).
2) Kubernetes control plane in VPC.
3) Redwood Private control plane components (operators, control API, console) deployed into redwood-system namespace.
4) Model-serving node pool: GPU nodes in serving namespace.
5) Internal LoadBalancer (service type: LoadBalancer with annotation for internal LB) exposing control plane APIs to customer app network.
6) Secrets stored in customer KMS; rollout uses a KMS provider integration.

Workshop flow and tasks:
(Pre-work) 1. Confirm cluster access and create namespaces: redwood-system, redwood-serving, redwood-monitoring
Commands:
kubectl create ns redwood-system redwood-serving redwood-monitoring

2. Install CRDs and operator (control plane) via Helm
helm repo add redwood https://helm.redwood.ai/charts
helm repo update
helm install redwood-operator redwood/redwood-operator -n redwood-system --wait --set ingress.internal=true --set operator.logLevel=info

Notes: operator.imageTag can be changed for specific release; --wait ensures CRDs are ready before proceeding.

3. Apply KMS & secrets configuration (example uses AWS KMS):
# create Kubernetes secret referencing KMS key alias (this example uses sealed secrets pattern or the redwood-kms plugin)
kubectl -n redwood-system create secret generic redwood-kms-config --from-literal=key_alias=alias/redwood-poc-kms
# if using IRSA/Workload Identity, ensure service account has decrypt permission

4. Deploy control-plane components (control API, console, config)
helm upgrade --install redwood-control redwood/redwood-control -n redwood-system \
  --set image.tag=v1.12.0 \
  --set service.type=LoadBalancer \
  --set service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/aws-load-balancer-internal"="true" \
  --set persistence.enabled=true \
  --wait

5. GPU node pool and serving runtime
- Provision a GPU node pool via cloud CLI (example: EKS):
eksctl create nodegroup --cluster=my-cluster --name=redwood-gpu --node-type=p4d.24xlarge --nodes=1 --nodes-min=1 --nodes-max=2 --asg-access
- Taint GPU nodes and create a serving DaemonSet/Deployment for the serving runtime:
# sample deployment overlay (use kustomize or helm values):
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redwood-serving-runtime
  namespace: redwood-serving
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redwood-serving-runtime
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redwood-serving-runtime
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - key: "node.kubernetes.io/accelerator"
        operator: "Exists"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: ghcr.io/redwood-inference/runtime:gpu-1.5.0
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
        env:
        - name: RW_RUNTIME_MODE
          value: "gpu"
        - name: RW_CONTROL_ENDPOINT
          value: "https://redwood-control.internal:8443"

6. Register a model and pin a rollout (demo):
# Create a Model CR (simplified YAML shown as a Helm value override example)
# Model: open-llama-7b, with two variants: fp16-gpu and int8-cpu-fallback
kubectl -n redwood-system apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: redwood.ai/v1
kind: ModelDeployment
metadata:
  name: demo-open-llama
spec:
  modelName: open-llama-7b
  variants:
    - name: gpu-fp16
      resources:
        gpu: 1
      image: ghcr.io/redwood-inference/models/open-llama-7b:fp16
    - name: cpu-int8
      resources:
        cpu: 8
      image: ghcr.io/redwood-inference/models/open-llama-7b:int8
  rollout:
    strategy: canary
    canary:
      weight: 10
      steps: 3
YAML

7. Sample inference client (Python) - verify model reachable and latency
# pip install requests
python
from time import time
import requests

RW_ENDPOINT = "https://redwood-control.internal/v1/generate"
API_KEY = "REPLACE_WITH_TEST_KEY"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
payload = {"model": "demo-open-llama:gpu-fp16", "input": "Write a short haiku about reliability"}
start = time()
resp = requests.post(RW_ENDPOINT, json=payload, headers=headers, verify=False)  # in lab environment internal certs may be self-signed
print("status", resp.status_code)
print("response", resp.json())
print("latency", time()-start)

8. Load test (basic) - burst check to validate autoscaling and batching
# Use a simple loop or vegeta/bash loop; example with bash and GNU parallel
seq 1 50 | parallel -j10 curl -s -X POST https://redwood-control.internal/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY}" -d '{"model":"demo-open-llama:gpu-fp16","input":"Hello"}' > /dev/null
# Monitor pods and GPU utilization during ramp
kubectl -n redwood-serving top pods

9. Observability and diagnostics
- Console: open the internal console URL (service LB IP) and check per-model token rates, batching efficiency, and latency percentiles.
- Tracing: ensure trace headers are propagated from the client and use the console trace view.
- Logs: operator logs in redwood-system show lifecycle events for ModelDeployment resources.

10. Troubleshooting common issues (cheat-sheet):
- Control API unreachable: confirm internal LB annotation and security group rules allow cluster subnets to reach LB.
- GPU not scheduling: check node labels/taints; confirm runtime image supports the installed CUDA driver.
- KMS decrypt errors: validate IAM role permissions and region alignment for KMS key.
- High latency at tail: reduce max-batch-wait or provision extra small-GPU replicas; validate prefix cache is enabled.

Workshop exercises (for customer teams):
A) Modify Values: change rollout canary weight and observe traffic shift in console.
B) Failover test: intentionally cordon GPU node, validate traffic moves to cpu-int8 variant with degraded latency but functional responses.
C) Cost vs latency: flip model variant to int8-cpu for 30% of traffic and measure cost delta using token-level cost breakdown.

Deliverables to customer at Handoff:
- Helm values file used in the workshop (save and attach)
- Short runbook: how to rotate KMS keys, scale serving nodepool, and add a new model variant
- Performance notes: observed p50/p95 for common prompt set and recommended autoscaling thresholds
- GitHub link with minimal example app that calls the private control plane

Appendix: example Helm values snippets (YAML as single-line comment for paste)
# values.yaml snippet for control chart
# image:
#   tag: v1.12.0
# service:
#   type: LoadBalancer
#   annotations:
#     service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-internal: "true"
# kms:
#   provider: aws
#   keyAlias: alias/redwood-poc-kms

Security considerations:
- Network: ensure control-plane LB only exposed to allowed CIDRs or internal VPC; consider PrivateLink for cross-account access.
- Secrets: prefer KMS + IAM roles, avoid static API keys.
- Audit: enable request audit logging and retain for compliance window.

Notes for SEs running the workshop:
- Pre-bake a short checklist for the customer that lists exact cloud quotas required for GPU nodes to avoid cloud provisioning delays.
- Bring a pre-built container image and backup manifests to recover quickly from infra issues.
- Use a small curated prompt set of 10–20 prompts for consistent benchmark numbers.
- Document any drift between helm chart defaults used here and customer's hardened policies.

Related artifacts and next steps:
- Link to full example repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/tree/main/redwood-private-k8s
- Follow-up: prepare deployment proposal for dedicated capacity if customer wants SLA-backed throughput after POC.

End of lab guide.

(Authors: Evelyn Park; review backlog: Miles Carter for infra checks, Anika Rao for security/KMS, Darren Liu for runtime tuning)
